title: The boy who wanted milk
hookLine: a poor boy who wanted milk becomes the sage who hands Krishna the names, and the names are gathered up as Mahadeva
carry: want the god himself, more than his gifts
tomorrow: what was carved under a stone in Kashmir?
last: KAPARDIN, THE FIERCE ONE WHO HEALS.

cards: A little boy wants milk. He's seen another child drink it, and he asks his mother. They're poor, living in a forest hermitage, and there's no milk to give.

So she stirs some flour into water and hands it to him. He drinks it, and knows it isn't milk. That small kitchen moment is where the Mahabharata begins the story of Upamanyu, the sage who handed Krishna Shiva's names.

teach.b: In the Mahabharata, Upamanyu tells Krishna his own story. When the boy cries over the flour and water, his mother tells him they have nothing, and that only Shiva can give what he's asking for.

So the boy sets out to worship Shiva, with his whole small life, in hard austerities. One day a visitor arrives: Indra, king of the gods, riding his white elephant, offering the boy any gift he wants.
Upamanyu turns him down. He wants nothing that doesn't come from Shiva. Then the visitor changes.
It was Shiva all along, testing him, and now Shiva shows himself, with Parvati beside him, and gives the boy far more than milk.
Years later, when Upamanyu has taught Krishna the names, Krishna worships Shiva, and Shiva and Parvati appear to him too, and grant his wish for a son. Notice what the story allows.
The boy began by asking for milk, Krishna came asking for a son, and neither is scolded. Hindus pray for things all the time: a recovery, an exam, a safe trip. But the story turns on Upamanyu's no.

teach.h: BHAKTI WANTS THE GOD, NOT THE GIFT.
teach.b: Offered anything by the king of the gods, he wants what comes from Shiva, and then, more than the gift, Shiva himself.
That runs all through bhakti, loving devotion: you may come to God for a cup of milk, and stay for God.
Across these days, a handful of names: Sthanu, Shankara, Pashupati, Nilakantha, Kapardin, and Vishnu's lotuses at every one.
One more name gathers them up: Mahadeva, the great god. Not great like a king who keeps his distance. Great like the one who turned up at a poor boy's hermitage, and answered him.

how: Devotees of Shiva address him as Mahadeva in daily speech and worship, and some recite his sahasranama in full on Mondays or on Maha Shivaratri, offering something at each name.

o: a prayer that poor families say when there's no milk at home
a hymn of Shiva's names, gathered up as Mahadeva, the great god
a list of gifts Indra offers to those who worship him

games.q: the names we gathered — tap the pairs.
p: granted his wish for a son

s: he turned Indra down; he wanted nothing that didn't come from Shiva.
the visitor on the white elephant was Shiva, testing him
the visitor changed, and Shiva showed himself with Parvati.
the names were first taught to Krishna by a king
in the Mahabharata, the sage Upamanyu teaches them to Krishna.

games.q: you're a boy who has worshipped Shiva for a long time. Indra, king of the gods, arrives and offers you any gift you want. what do you say?
o: take the gift: Indra is a great god too.
say no: you want nothing that isn't from Shiva.
games.why: Upamanyu says no. the visitor turns out to be Shiva, testing him, and Shiva shows himself.

practice: Let the names you've met pass through your mind, one per breath, like beads on a string: Sthanu, steady; Shankara, well-being; Pashupati, the loosened rope; Nilakantha, the held poison; Kapardin, the healer; Mahadeva.
Notice which one you linger on; that's the one that's yours for now. If you pray, say that name a few times, slowly, asking for nothing; if you don't, just rest with the word.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Sahasranama. The hymn of Shiva's names, taught by Upamanyu, the boy who wanted milk, and gathered up today as Mahadeva, the great god.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Mahadeva, the great (maha) god (deva); a name of Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: want the god himself, more than his gifts. A poor boy asked for milk and was given Mahadeva. That's today, done.
